summary: The trader picked 1,476 of 5,479 planned resting orders. Only 2 of them filled, and together they earned $0.51 (conservative accounting), almost all of it from one fully hedged Troy vs LSU wcbb totals order. The 4,003 skipped plans would have filled 5 times and earned $0.36 at the trader's size, so skipping cost $0.36 rather than saving anything. All three rankings tie the trader's picks at $0.51, and the perfect-hindsight ceiling is $0.55, so ranking left at most $0.04 on the table. The hedger and gap data show nothing for the day (0 fast-hedger fills seen, 0 gaps), so the 5-minute simulation cannot be compared against anything.
root_causes: This day is mostly about fill rate. There were 7 fills across 5,479 plans and every one was hedged (no unhedged leftovers, no open bags), so no fill went one-sided and no luck from leftovers is in the numbers. The $0.51 is a single fill, which is noise and not evidence of skill. One Podziemski points prop filled and was hedged at about $0, which fits an edge that is thin after fees and conservative hedge pricing. One order was pulled because the hedge moved. Most of the skipping came from sizing caps, not edge quality: 2,728 plans were rejected as too few contracts after caps and 1,195 for edge below the minimum after resize. The skipped plans that filled were small totals and margin orders worth $0.02-$0.18 each. The learner is not calibrated. The model trained only on earlier outcomes predicted -0.018 c/contract on average against an actual +0.001, rank correlation was -0.029 (no better than random), and the lowest-predicted bin had the most fills and the highest actual value. With 7 fills, none of these calibration numbers mean much yet.
what_to_change: Proposal: the cap rule 'too few contracts after caps' rejected 2,728 plans, half of everything. Review whether the per-leg cost caps ($10, or $5 for props) together with the minimum contract count are screening out cheap totals and margin orders that do fill, before changing anything.

Proposal: give the learner score little or no weight in ranking until its out-of-sample rank correlation stays positive over several days. Today it was -0.029 and added nothing over biggest-edge ordering.

Proposal: check that the Oracle hedger's fast_hedges.csv and gap_episodes.csv are actually being collected for this window. Zero fills and zero gaps on a day with 7 simulated fills means the hedger comparison is blind.

hypotheses.statement: Resting orders on game totals (nba/cbb/wcbb) fill at a materially higher rate per plan than player props and moneylines.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv, group resolved plans by market kind over all available days and compare fills per plan, with binomial confidence intervals. Check whether totals stay above props once the count reaches 30 or more fills.

hypotheses.statement: Plans rejected as 'too few contracts after caps' have a positive average value per plan when sized at the minimum allowed contracts.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Join trader_orders.csv rejection reasons to maker_outcomes.csv, then sum the conservative value of those plans at the minimum contract size over all days and compare it with the taken plans' value per plan.

hypotheses.statement: The learner's predicted value per contract is anti-correlated or uncorrelated with realized fill probability, because its training outcomes are dominated by non-fills.
hypotheses.how_to_test: For each day, refit on prior outcomes only and compute the rank correlation of predictions with fill (0/1) and, separately, with value given a fill, using maker_outcomes.csv. Check whether either correlation is consistently positive.

lesson: With 7 fills in about 5,500 plans, every order that filled was hedged cleanly; the bottleneck is fill rate and sizing caps, not ranking or hedging.

summary: The trader picked 1,457 plans. One filled, a hedged Michigan St. vs Tennessee cbb margin order worth $0.23. On paper, skipped plans would have earned $9.52, but $9.44 of that is one unhedged Tennessee St. vs Louisville wcbb margin leftover that happened to win. Leave that out and the skipped side is about $0.08. All three rankings tie the trader at $0.23, and the hindsight ceiling is $0.28, so the ceiling sits only $0.05 above what was actually picked. The Oracle hedger saw 1 fill and fully hedged it, matching the 5-minute simulation (1 pair). The server timed 205 instant-hedge gaps with a median of 59s (140 lasted 30s or more), but none were catchable.
root_causes: Luck is most of today's headline. The $9.52 'cost of skipping' is almost all one one-sided fill (Tennessee St. vs Louisville, 16 contracts) whose leftover settled as a win. An unhedged leftover can lose just as easily, so this is not evidence that skipping was a mistake. A second unhedged skipped fill (Mamukelashvili rebounds) lost $0.05. The fills that were hedged were all small, -$0.04 to +$0.23, which fits edges that are thin after fees and conservative hedge pricing. Two of the three prop fills were flat or negative. Fill rate stays tiny: 6 fills across 6,221 plans. Rejections are again dominated by 'too few contracts after caps' (3,413) and 'edge below minimum after resize' (1,312). The learner is not calibrated. Out of sample it predicted -0.031 c/contract against an actual +0.010, rank correlation was -0.005 (no signal), and the top bin's +0.047 actual comes from a single fill. Two days of near-zero rank correlation is consistent, but there are still too few fills to judge the learner.
what_to_change: Proposal: report take/skip in the post-mortem both with and without unhedged leftovers. One lucky leftover turned 'skipping cost $0.08' into 'skipping cost $9.52' and could mislead anyone tuning the rules.

Proposal: look at why 205 gaps with a median length of 59s produced zero catchable ones. Check whether the catchable test (depth, fees, size) is too strict or whether the gaps are mostly unfillable depth, before acting on gap speed.

hypotheses.statement: Fills on wcbb/cbb margin (spread) markets go unhedged more often than fills on other market kinds, because the Polymarket US hedge depth on those markets is thin or disappears.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv (joined with maker_bags.csv), compute the unhedged share of fills by sport and market kind over all days, and compare spread vs totals vs props with confidence intervals.

hypotheses.statement: Most instant-hedge gaps that last 30s or more are not catchable because of insufficient depth at the quoted price, not because of fees.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In the hedger's gap_episodes.csv, split the 30s+ episodes by the reason they failed the catchable test (depth vs net edge after fees) and tabulate the reasons over all days.

lesson: A single lucky unhedged leftover can swamp a day's take-vs-skip numbers; judge decisions on the hedged fills only.

summary: The trader picked 2,099 plans. One filled, a hedged Bowling Green vs Penn St. wcbb margin order worth $0.21. The skipped plans would have filled 4 times for $0.16 at the trader's size, so skipping cost $0.16. Every alternative ranking, including the trader's own formula re-run, reached $0.37, which equals the hindsight ceiling. That leaves the actual picks $0.16 short, a gap that probably comes from capital already tied up or the timing of picks rather than from the ordering itself. The Oracle hedger saw 4 fills (3 of them on plans the trader picked) with a median of 3s from fill to hedge, but only 25% were fully hedged and it locked $0.01. That is a much worse picture than the 5-minute simulation, which recorded 1 taken fill; only 1 pair could be compared directly, and it matched. The server timed 1,176 gaps with a median of 190s, and none were catchable.
root_causes: There is no luck component today: all 5 simulated fills were hedged and no leftovers are open. Results are small and edge-thin. Fills were worth -$0.07 to +$0.21, the Caleb Martin assists prop lost $0.07 after hedging, and one of the three Houston vs Kansas margin fills was worth $0.00. Rejections moved toward 'edge below minimum after resize' (1,595) over 'too few contracts after caps' (1,063), and 189 plans were too close to start. The main finding is a disagreement between data sources. The live-speed hedger recorded 3 fills on the trader's picks where the simulation scored 1, and it fully hedged only 1 of its 4, so the simulation may be overstating both how clean the hedges are and how rare fills are. With 4 fills this is only a signal. The learner is still uncalibrated for a third day: out of sample it predicted -0.017 c/contract against an actual +0.001, rank correlation was -0.024, and the highest-predicted bin had zero fills.
what_to_change: Proposal: reconcile the trader-picked fills in the hedger's fast_hedges.csv against maker_outcomes.csv for this day (3 vs 1) before trusting either source's fill counts. Today only 1 pair could be compared.

Proposal: three days in a row the learner's out-of-sample rank correlation has been between -0.03 and 0. Consider giving it zero weight in the ranking formula until it shows a positive correlation, keeping in mind that the total fill count is still very small.

hypotheses.statement: Fills seen by the Oracle fast hedger are fully hedged less often than the 5-minute simulation assumes for the same kind of plans.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Across all days, compare the fully hedged share in fast_hedges.csv with the hedged share of fills in maker_outcomes.csv, grouped by sport and market kind. Report per-pair agreement wherever the same fill appears in both.

hypotheses.statement: The trader's actual picks underperform its own formula re-ranked from scratch because capital already tied up in earlier resting orders blocks later, better plans.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Using trader_orders.csv and maker_outcomes.csv, for each run compare the value of the actual picks with the formula's unconstrained re-pick, and correlate the shortfall with the Kalshi budget already committed at that run.

lesson: When the live hedger and the simulation disagree on fills and hedge rates, fix the measurement before tuning the strategy.

summary: The trader's picks earned $1.21 from 4 fills out of 3,110 picked plans. All 4 were game totals, all hedged, and 3 of them were in just two women's college basketball games. Skipping cost $0.19 (4 skipped plans filled and hedged for small amounts). Every ranking tied the hindsight ceiling at $1.21, so the order of picks did not matter today. The Oracle hedger saw 10 fills, hedged all of them in a median of 6 seconds, and agreed with the 5-minute simulation on all 3 shared fills. Of 168 instant-hedge gaps, 135 lasted 30 seconds or more, but only 1 was catchable, and it was worth $0.00.
root_causes: Luck versus decisions: nothing went one-sided and no leftovers were left open, so today's result is small but clean. Still, 4 taken fills (7 hedged fills overall) are far too few to judge any decision, and they are clustered: Radford vs Tennessee alone gave $0.73 of the $1.21, so one game's flow drove the day. Thin edges and caps were the binding limits, not ranking. 12,382 plans were rejected as too few contracts after caps and 2,307 as edge below minimum after resize, while every ranking reached the ceiling. Learner: not calibrated and not useful for ranking. It predicted -0.021c per contract against an actual +0.001c, with rank correlation -0.028. All 7 fills landed in the lowest-predicted bin, the fourth day in a row with a slightly negative correlation (-0.029, -0.005, -0.024, -0.028). Its scores currently add nothing over plain edge.
what_to_change: Proposal: give the learner score zero weight in the trader's formula until its rank correlation turns positive across several days. On all four reviewed days it has been flat or negative, and today every ranking, including plain biggest edge first, tied the ceiling.
Proposal: when counting results, treat fills from the same game as one data point. Today 5 of 7 hedged fills came from two games, so per-fill statistics overstate the sample size.

hypotheses.statement: Fills cluster within games: once one plan on a game fills, other plans on the same game are much more likely to fill that day, so the effective sample size is the number of distinct games with fills, not the number of fills.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv, over all days, compare the fill rate of plans on games that had at least one other fill that day with the rate on games that had none. Also count distinct games versus fills per day.

hypotheses.statement: Plans rejected as 'edge too good to be real (bad quote?)' are mostly genuine bad quotes: they fill rarely or lose value when they do, so the filter is protecting the trader.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Join the trader_orders.csv rows with that rejection reason to maker_outcomes.csv over all days and compare their fill rate, hedged share and conservative value per plan with the taken plans.

lesson: Four clean hedged fills from two games tied every ranking with the ceiling, so the day says nothing about ranking skill; the learner is still anti-calibrated and the binding limits are fill rate and caps.

summary: The trader's picks earned $0.22 from a single hedged fill (a 20-contract Little Rock vs Oklahoma St. wcbb total), out of 3,470 planned orders. Skipping cost $0.06: the 6,766 skipped plans had 3 hedged fills (one Tyrese Proctor PRA prop, two Boston vs Sacramento margins) worth $0.06 at the trader's size. All four rankings and the hindsight ceiling tied at $0.22, so the ranking choice made no difference today. The Oracle hedger saw 5 fills, all fully hedged with a 3s median, but again no fill could be matched to the 5-minute simulation (0 pairs); of 328 instant-hedge gaps, 273 lasted 30s or more yet only 1 was catchable, worth $0.07.
root_causes: There is nothing to separate luck from skill here: one taken fill and three skipped fills, all hedged, no one-sided fills and no open leftovers, so the day is noise for deciding anything. The limit is still fill rate (4 fills from about 10,200 plans) plus sizing caps: 'too few contracts after caps' (3,832) and 'edge below minimum after resize' (2,686) were the main rejection reasons, and the skipped fills that did happen were worth only cents. The learner is still not calibrated. It predicted -0.013 c per contract against an actual 0.000, the rank correlation was -0.012 (about zero, negative for the fourth day in a row), and fills landed in the lowest and highest predicted bins alike. Its scores carry no ranking information yet. The hedger and the simulation still cannot be compared because none of their fills match up, which has now happened two days running.
what_to_change: Proposal: fix or explain the join between fast_hedges.csv and maker_outcomes.csv before reading anything into hedger-vs-simulation numbers. Two days in a row have had several fills on each side but 0 matched pairs.

Proposal: keep the learner score's weight in the trader's formula small, or at zero, until its rank correlation is positive over a multi-day window. Four days in a row it has been near zero or negative.

hypotheses.statement: Plans rejected for 'too few contracts after caps' fill and hedge at about the same rate as taken plans, so that rejection costs meaningful value over many days even though it costs only cents on any one day.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Join trader_orders.csv rows with that rejection reason to maker_outcomes.csv across all days. Compare fill rate, hedged share and conservative value per plan (at the trader's size) against taken plans, with confidence intervals.

hypotheses.statement: The same Kalshi fill is attributed to more than one plan (for example, plans repeated across runs on the same market), so fill counts and skipped value are inflated by duplicates.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv, group fills by market, side, price and fill time across all days, and count how many groups hold more than one plan row. Recompute daily fills and value after deduplicating.

lesson: One hedged taken fill tied every ranking with the ceiling, so the day shows nothing about decision quality; the real problems are still the fill rate, a learner with no ranking signal, and a hedger-to-simulation join that matches nothing.

summary: The trader's 4,710 picks produced one fill (9 contracts of Dalton Kincaid rec_yds, hedged) worth $0.08 under conservative accounting. Skipping cost $0.13: the one skipped fill (7 Carson Beck pass_yds contracts) was hedged and would have earned more than the trader's own pick. Every ranking, including the hindsight ceiling, came to $0.08, so the day tells us nothing about ranking skill. The Oracle hedger saw 4 fills, hedged all of them with a 4-second median, and locked $0.58. Of 387 instant-hedge gaps, 312 lasted 30 s or more but only 1 was catchable, worth $0.07.
root_causes: Two hedged fills in total, both NFL props, is noise, so nothing here separates luck from decision quality. No fill went one-sided and no leftover was open. The Carson Beck fill was skipped, and the simulation marked it UNHEDGED while the hedger hedged it (+$0.37 reconciled). That gap is a measurement difference, not a trading decision. The binding constraints are again the fill rate (2 fills over about 15,000 plans) and sizing: 7,802 rejections were 'too few contracts after caps' and 2,646 were 'edge below minimum after resize'. The learner is still not calibrated and has no ranking signal: it predicted -0.013 c per contract against an actual 0.000, with a rank correlation of -0.018. Both fills landed in the lowest-predicted bin. That is the fourth day in a row with a slightly negative correlation, but with so few fills the error bars are huge.
what_to_change: Proposal: notable_fills lists each fill twice (Kincaid and Beck each appear two times). Check whether the post-mortem's fill listing, or the outcome rows behind it, double-count before trusting fill counts. This ties to the open 2026-11-20 duplicate-attribution hypothesis.

Proposal: the learner's rank correlation has been slightly negative on all four reviewed days (-0.024, -0.028, -0.012, -0.018). Consider giving the learner score zero weight in the trader's formula until it shows a positive correlation over a pooled multi-day sample.

hypotheses.statement: Most instant-hedge gaps that last 30 s or more are not catchable because resting-order depth at the gap price is too small for even the minimum trader size, not because they close too fast.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In gap_episodes.csv across all days, for gaps that lasted 30 s or more, compare the available size with the trader's minimum contracts after caps. Report what share fail on size, what share fail on duration, and what share fail on edge after fees.

hypotheses.statement: Fills where the 5-minute simulation says UNHEDGED but the fast hedger hedged are concentrated in props whose Polymarket hedge moved within the 5-minute window, so the simulation systematically understates prop value.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Join fast_hedges.csv with maker_outcomes.csv on market, side and fill time across all days. For pairs where the statuses disagree, tabulate by market kind and by Polymarket price movement between the fill and the next 5-minute snapshot.

lesson: Two hedged prop fills tied every ranking with the ceiling, so the day shows no decision skill; the skipped fill earned more than the taken one, and the learner's ranking signal is still slightly negative for a fourth straight day.

summary: The trader's picks earned $0.04 on 4 fills out of 3,386 taken plans: one taken hedged prop (Landry Shamet points, +$0.14) covered one taken hedged prop that lost (Bam Adebayo rebounds, -$0.11), and one taken fill was left unhedged. The 6,241 skipped plans would have lost $0.04 at the trader's size, so skipping saved $0.04, and all plans at full research size would have come to -$0.38, which is a research number, not money anyone could have made. Every ranking tied the hindsight ceiling at $0.04, so the day says nothing about which ranking is better. The fast hedger fully hedged only 79% of the 9 fills it shared with the 5-minute simulation, against 99% in the simulation, and of 630 instant-hedge gaps (520 lasting 30 s or more) only 1 was catchable, worth $0.02.
root_causes: Luck dominates: the day's net comes down to two taken props, one winner and one loser, and with 4 taken fills the total is noise. The Adebayo loss happened on a hedged fill, which points to a thin edge being wiped out when the hedge is priced at the worse of the book and the price at fill, not to a bad pick. One of the moves came from the Bobby Portis fill, which the simulation counted as hedged but the hedger only partly hedged. That and the 79% vs 99% gap suggest the 5-minute simulation is too optimistic about hedge depth on this day, though 9 pairs is too few to be sure. The binding limits are still sizing and edge: 3,795 rejections for too few contracts after caps and 2,364 for edge below minimum after resize. The learner is still not calibrated. It predicts -0.012 c per contract on average against an actual 0.0, its bins are nearly flat (-0.045 to +0.002 predicted, all about 0 actual), and its rank correlation is 0.003, the fifth day in a row with no ranking signal. No plans fell in skip groups, so the learner did not change any decision.
what_to_change: Proposal: treat the 5-minute simulation's hedged share as an upper bound when judging hedged fills, and report hedger-reconciled values as the main number, since on 9 shared fills the real hedger fully hedged 79% versus the simulation's 99%. Confirm over more days before relying on it.

Proposal: keep the learner advisory only (no skip groups, no change to the trader's formula) until its rank correlation is clearly positive over several days. It has now been near zero or negative for five straight days.

Proposal: check whether hedged fills near the 2c minimum edge end up negative after hedge slippage, as Adebayo did, before considering any change to min_edge_c. One day is not enough to change the rule.

hypotheses.statement: Hedged fills whose planned edge is close to the 2c minimum often end with negative conservative value, because the hedge price moves against the order between planning and fill, so realized locked profit per contract falls well below the planned edge.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv across all days, for hedged fills, regress or bin realized value per contract on planned edge (cents). Report the share of hedged fills with negative value in each planned-edge bin (for example 2-3c, 3-5c, 5c+).

hypotheses.statement: On fills both systems saw, the fast hedger ends PARTIAL or UNHEDGED more often than the 5-minute simulation because Polymarket depth at the hedge price is smaller at fill time than the simulation's snapshot assumes, concentrated in player props.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Join fast_hedges.csv with maker_outcomes.csv on market, side and fill time across all days. For pairs where the simulation says hedged and the hedger says PARTIAL or UNHEDGED, compare the hedged contracts with the filled contracts and tabulate by market kind.

lesson: Four taken fills netted $0.04 because one lucky prop offset one hedged loser; every ranking tied the ceiling, the learner still has no ranking signal, and the real hedger hedged noticeably less than the 5-minute simulation assumes.

summary: The trader's picks filled 7 times, all hedged, for +$1.54 conservative value; most of that came from four 18-contract fills on the Belmont vs LSU women's basketball total. Skipping saved $4.89: nearly all of it is one skipped Stephon Castle assists prop that filled and could not be hedged (-$4.90 at the trader's size). Every ranking (biggest edge, edge per dollar, the trader's formula) tied the actual picks at $1.54, $0.04 below the $1.58 hindsight ceiling, so the ordering did not matter today. The fast hedger saw 20 fills with a 4 s median and 95% fully hedged, but on the 10 fills both systems saw it hedged 82% vs the simulation's 94%; reconciling moved value by +$2.17, mostly a Belmont-LSU fill the simulation called PARTIAL that the hedger fully hedged, and only 1 of 429 gaps was catchable ($0.01).
root_causes: Decision quality is hard to separate from luck with 7 taken fills, and those are concentrated in one game, so they are really closer to one correlated observation than seven. The positive day came from hedges that locked at small positive edges (3c-66c per fill), not from leftovers, so there was no unhedged luck in the taken picks. The big avoided loss was a prop where hedge depth was not there at fill time: a one-sided fill, not a pricing mistake by the trader, and the skip was driven by the rules ('too few contracts after caps' and 'edge below minimum after resize' account for most of the 6,575 rejections), not by any forecast that the prop would go unhedged. The learner is not calibrated for ranking: the predicted level is close (-0.008c vs -0.004c per contract), but rank correlation is -0.042, the fifth straight day near zero or negative. Its lowest-predicted bin held 9 of the 10 fills and was the only bin with a non-zero actual (-0.021c vs -0.03c predicted), so what it captures is mostly which plans get filled at all, not which ones are good.
what_to_change: Proposal: track contracts filled per event within a day. Four 18-contract fills landed on one Belmont vs LSU total, so a per-event exposure cap could be worth considering if this clustering repeats over several days. One day is not enough to set a number.

Proposal: since the fast hedger and the 5-minute simulation keep disagreeing (82% vs 94% hedged today, and reconciliation changed value by +$2.17), treat reconciled hedger status as the main value for fills both systems saw when judging days, and keep the simulation as a fallback only.

Proposal: keep the learner's score at low or zero weight in the trader's formula until its rank correlation turns clearly positive over a multi-day window. Five days in, it has shown no ranking signal.

hypotheses.statement: The learner's predicted value per contract mostly predicts whether a plan gets filled (adverse selection): the lowest-predicted bins hold most fills, and among filled plans alone, predicted value has no rank correlation with realized value.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Across all days in maker_outcomes.csv, refit the learner on outcomes before each day (as the post-mortem does), bin plans by predicted value, and report fill rate per bin. Then compute the rank correlation between predicted and realized value per contract using filled plans only.

hypotheses.statement: Fills on totals in college basketball (wcbb/ncaab) earn higher hedged value per contract than NBA totals and props, because their Polymarket hedge books move less between planning and fill.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv joined with maker_bags.csv across all days, group hedged fills by sport and market kind. Compare conservative value per contract, hedged share and fill count per group, with bootstrap intervals, and check the Polymarket price change from fill to hedge in fast_hedges.csv for the same groups.

lesson: Today's $1.54 came from one game's totals, and the $4.89 saved came from the rules skipping a prop that went unhedged, so neither shows ranking skill. Every ordering again tied, and the learner still has no rank signal.

summary: The trader's picks filled twice and earned $0.01, essentially nothing. Skipping saved $8.73: the 15 skipped fills would have lost that much at the trader's size, almost all of it ($8.97) from one Notre Dame vs West Virginia women's college game and a Daniss Jenkins PRA prop that ended partial or unhedged. Every ranking scored the same $0.01 against a hindsight ceiling of $0.08, so ordering made no real difference on a day with only 2-3 fills in the budget. The Oracle hedger saw 38 fills and hedged 97% fully with a 3 s median, locking $5.25 at research size; reconciling it with the 5-minute simulation changed 6 statuses for +$0.65, and none of the 80 instant-hedge gaps were catchable.
root_causes: Decision quality cannot be judged from 2 taken fills worth $0.01. The $8.73 saved was the rules (mostly 'too few contracts after caps', 4,921 rejections) keeping the trader out of fills that went one-sided, not ranking skill. Those losses came from fills that went partial or unhedged and were then counted at full cost, which is what conservative accounting does. The +$1.62 and +$2.03 unhedged prop leftovers that won (John Collins, Daniss Jenkins points) were luck, not edge. The positive $33.29 full-size number is a research figure and is not what real money would have made. The reconcile examples show the same plans (Daniss Jenkins, the WVU leg) flipping both ways between sim and hedger, which suggests the fill pairing may be ambiguous and needs checking before the +$0.65 is trusted. Gaps lasted a median of 126 s and 57 lasted 30 s or more, yet none were catchable, so duration is not what blocks them. The learner is not calibrated: it predicted +0.004c per contract against an actual -0.015c, with rank correlation -0.02. Its lowest-predicted bin held 14 of the 17 fills (actual -0.074c), and its top bin got 3 fills that earned about zero.
what_to_change: Proposal: before using reconcile numbers in decisions, check the hedger-vs-simulation fill matching. Today the same Daniss Jenkins and WVU plans appear as both 'sim UNHEDGED, hedger hedged' and 'sim hedged, hedger UNHEDGED', which points to duplicate or mismatched pairs.

Proposal: keep the learner's score out of the ranking (or give it zero weight) until its rank correlation turns positive over several days. It has been near zero or negative for five straight post-mortems, and today it changed nothing versus biggest-edge-first.

hypotheses.statement: The reconcile step double-counts or mismatches fills when one market and side has several fills (or partial fills) close together, so status disagreements come in symmetric pairs that cancel out rather than reflecting real hedging differences.
hypotheses.how_to_test: Join fast_hedges.csv with maker_outcomes.csv on market, side and fill time across all days. Count market/side keys with more than one fill within the matching window, and check whether the status disagreements cluster on those keys and come in opposite-direction pairs.

hypotheses.statement: Game-level (moneyline/margin) fills in college basketball that land close to tip-off end PARTIAL or UNHEDGED far more often than earlier fills, because Polymarket hedge depth thins out near the start.
hypotheses.how_to_test: In maker_outcomes.csv across all days, for moneyline/margin fills, bin by minutes from fill to game start and compare the hedged/partial/unhedged shares and conservative value per contract per bin. Use the start time from trader_orders.csv or the plan data, and compare college sports with NBA.

hypotheses.statement: Positive full-size research value on days with negative trader-size value comes mostly from a few unhedged leftovers that happened to settle as winners, not from locked hedge profit.
hypotheses.how_to_test: For each day, split full-size value in maker_outcomes.csv joined with maker_bags.csv into locked hedge profit and settled leftover profit. Report the share coming from leftovers and how much the top three leftovers contribute.

lesson: Skipping saved $8.73 because the rules kept the trader out of one-sided college moneyline and prop fills, not because of ranking skill. With 2 taken fills worth $0.01, every ranking tied, and the learner still has no rank signal.
